prompts.prompt: Use case: stylized-concept. Production game sprite atlas for an isometric Star Trek Borg cube theme in Agent Watch. Create EXACTLY NINE full-body poses of ONE adult Borg drone, arranged in a perfectly regular 3-column by 3-row grid, square 1536x1536 canvas. Each cell exactly one separate complete figure, centered horizontally, feet baseline 90% down cell, same camera, body proportions and scale throughout. True transparent alpha background and transparent gutters, no floor, no checkerboard pixels, no text, labels or borders. Detailed polished sci-fi game illustration, realistic humanoid proportions slightly simplified for reading at 90px high, crisp silhouette, subtle painterly metal surfaces. Black graphite ribbed biomechanical armor, exposed pale organic face, embedded cybernetics, cables and tubes, small luminous Borg green emitters, restrained warm metal highlights. Classic First Contact / Voyager Borg aesthetic, not cute robots and not pixel art. Camera orthographic 3/4 elevated about 25 degrees. Pose order left-to-right top-to-bottom: 1 neutral standing facing viewer slightly to right, 2 same front-facing drone walking with left leg forward, 3 same front-facing drone walking with right leg forward; 4 back-view walking left leg forward, 5 back-view walking right leg forward, 6 front-facing operating a control panel with one arm reaching forward (no panel drawn); 7 same operating pose with arm moved, 8 front-facing taking a careful backward step with torso rigid and face toward viewer, 9 upright regeneration stance, feet together, arms relaxed downward, natural eye closed and implant dim. Entire body fits each cell with generous empty margin. No weapons firing, no blood or wounds. Identity: A broad adult masculine tactical drone, very pale skin, bald scalp partly covered by a heavy asymmetrical black cranial plate, ONE vivid red optical lens on the left side of the face, thick ribbed chest armor, right forearm a blunt multi-tool claw, stout mechanical legs. Distinct silhouette: wide squared shoulders.

Use case: stylized-concept. Production isometric game artwork for a Star Trek Borg cube theme. Detailed polished sci-fi game illustration with crisp readable silhouettes, black graphite biomechanical machinery, ribbed hoses, aged gunmetal and copper detail, luminous emerald green accents, subtle silver rim lighting. Orthographic 3/4 elevated view around 25 degrees, consistent scale. True transparent alpha outside each object, no opaque background or checkerboard pixels, no lettering, labels, watermarks or grid lines. Create one animation atlas of the BORG QUEEN, EXACTLY 12 full-body frames in a regular 4-column by 3-row grid on a 2048x1536 landscape canvas. Same Queen in all frames: bald very pale head and shoulders, dark subtle veins/cranial implants, recognizable regal First Contact Borg Queen silhouette, sleek fully covered black ribbed synthetic body, slender mechanical limbs, nonsexual neutral presentation. All frames share the same centered body size, feet at 90% of cell, stable scale, empty margins. No throne or ground, no other characters. Row1 left to right: neutral standing facing viewer; right hand beginning a commanding gesture; both arms raised commanding the collective; arm lowering to her side. Row2: head and upper torso turning toward screen-left to scan; head and upper torso turning screen-right to scan; reaching one hand forward with small green holographic rings around palm; both hands drawing the rings inward in a communication gesture. Row3: mechanical reassembly sequence, visibly synthetic machinery with NO gore: pale head and upper shoulders hovering above the empty synthetic body connected by an extended metal spinal shaft; head/shoulders lowering toward torso on a partly compressed shaft; head and shoulders fully seated into synthetic body with arms slightly spread; connected Queen standing still with eyes closed. Keep feet/body base in the same position and keep total frame extent inside the cell. Mechanical gaps and connectors only, no blood or wounds. The last four must clearly depict progressive reassembly, not four identical poses.
